Two problems occur when employees openly discuss wages. First, employees may find out that just because Joe is better looking or friends with the management he gets a higher salary by a significant amount. Second, employees who under perform see the employees that try harder and perform better making more money. This often leads to a mentality of 'We have the same job title and should get paid the same!' Alternatively, people with seniority who have been there for a while may make less than some freshly-hired person with little experience. This is usually caused by the going rate for those positions surpassing the annual raises given.

Employers don't want to deal with those problems by giving equal pay, since that would cost quite a bit more. Instead, they think keeping people in the dark is likely to make them happier. I think there must be a better way to be transparent and fair, yet still have a profitable business.

I would solve these problems by making base salaries standard across positions, so nobody is able to negotiate more than someone else. Every 6 months have a round of raises for those who can show improvement and solid work. I would be open with each round of raises and have information regarding why decisions were made available to all employees.

At first employees may feel like it wasn't fair to be treated equally, but as time went on, the valuable employees would see raises and those who could not keep up would try harder, accept the fact that they are under performing, or leave so I could find someone better.

A lot of people here are saying companies do it just so they can save money, pay most people less and engage in nepotism or other forms of favoritism. While I do not disagree all of those things do happen in real life, that is far too simplistic a view. Those are side effects, not the primary reason.

What most companies care most about is not just spending less per se, but maximizing results while minimizing costs. So, they pay people more when they believe that will achieve the corporate goal and less when they believe that will do it.

Most people tend to overestimate their own competence and abilities while underestimating other people. So, think about what happens if you let everyone know what everyone else is paid, how big their raise was, how big their bonus was, etc.

If you just straight forwardly pay your high performers better, a lot of other people will be upset because they will not believe they are lower performers. They'll blame favoritism or something else. If you pay everyone lockstep, those who are doing more and better work will resent it because they know they are being artifically paid less than they are worth so that others can be paid more than they are worth.

Publicizing pay data is a lose/lose from the company's perspective. And that is only from consideration of the internal workings of a company viewed in isolation. Companies compete with each other in the market for labor. Information across an industry can have the same negative affects on a work force as the information being shared within the company, but with the added problem of potentially harming the company in the marketplace by increasing its costs and lowering its productivity while it tries to keep its best employees happy without losing lesser, but necessary employees, in the face of competitive pressure from rival firms.
And yet, most companies have performance reviews...

True, but they don't generally share those with everyone, either. They also often have rating systems where the average is artificially high, such that on a 5 point scale, the average is closer to a 4 than a 3. There are a lot of different reasons for that, though. Some is intentional to help morale (similar to the compensation information concerns), but a lot is due to managers using grade inflation for their own people (often subconsciously). It can take a lot of work to be fair to everyone to account for such bias and it often means increasing scores rather than decreasing them.
